questions.expected_answer: Its gradient with respect to the logit carries a factor p(1-p), which vanishes when the model is confidently wrong (about 1000x smaller than cross-entropy's at z = -8). Binary cross-entropy's gradient is p - y, so confident errors still get a strong push.

answer.answer: MSE is a poor loss for a sigmoid classifier because its gradient carries the extra chain-rule factor p(1-p) from the sigmoid's own derivative, which vanishes when the model is confidently wrong (saturated), so learning stalls; cross-entropy cancels this factor exactly, giving dL/dz = p - y, whose push is largest when the model is most wrong. For example, at z = -8 with y = 1 the MSE gradient is about 0.00067 while the cross-entropy gradient is about 0.9997.

answer.answer: For softmax cross-entropy, the gradient with respect to the logits is p - onehot(y), i.e., the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot true label; for example, with p ≈ (0.665, 0.245, 0.090) and true class 0 it equals (-0.335, 0.245, 0.090), so only the true class gets a negative entry. This is the same p - y form as the binary sigmoid case, where sigmoid plus binary cross-entropy gives dL/dz = p - y, with the sigmoid derivative canceling against the log so the push stays proportional to the probability error (the binary formula being the C = 2 case).
